title: Memory Sandwich & Cross-Kernel Flow Control — Prototype Notes
content:
Purpose
This note captures an experimental approach for coordinating execution and memory ownership across multiple kernel backends (TensorRT, Triton, custom kernels) without global pauses or heavyweight copy fences. We call the idea a "memory sandwich" — lightweight layered ownership plus a flow-control shim that enforces backpressure and graceful fallback between heterogeneous execution stages.

Context / motivation
- We frequently see performance cliffs when moving between fast fused kernels (TensorRT) and slower CPU/custom-kernel steps: GPU memory copy stalls, KV cache misses that force synchronous host roundtrips, and unpredictable tail latency from kernel load/unload.
- Existing heuristics (kernel-affinity by model family + static batching) are necessary but insufficient when workloads mix streaming short-chat requests, long-context decode, and occasional rerank/embedding ops.
- Goal: avoid full model fallback and avoid large synchronous copies while preserving SLOs for short-tail token latency.

Core concepts (high-level)
1) Memory sandwich: ephemeral ownership layers for tensors and KV-state. The runtime tracks three logical layers per request:
   - Soft-owner (producer): kernel that last produced/updated a tensor; allowed to modify in-place under a lease.
   - Shared-borrow: read-only borrow view for downstream kernels that do not mutate state. Implemented via GPU memory aliasing when safe, otherwise copy-on-write.
   - Eviction/Transfer slot: small reserved staging area (pinned host memory or device scratch slab) used to transfer ownership without blocking entire device.
2) Flow-control shim (lightweight): a cross-kernel coordinator that enforces per-device and per-stream backpressure using token buckets and request-level latency budgets. It mediates when a kernel may take an ownership lease and when it must use the staging slot.
3) Preflight affinity probe: a non-blocking micro-probe that samples current kernel load, estimated KV cache hit-prob, and recent kernel latency to decide execution placement.

Why this differs from naive approaches
- Avoids global stop-the-world: instead of pausing other requests to migrate memory, we stage only the affected tensor(s) into a bounded transfer slot.
- Keeps fast-path for short requests: short token sequences can stay within their initial kernel if the probe predicts <5ms incremental decode cost.
- Provides graceful fallback: when affinity probe detects sustained overload, requests are routed to a compatible, lower-footprint kernel variant (quantized/custom) with a predictable transfer path.

Prototype architecture (components)
- Sandwich allocator: small allocator that reserves per-GPU transfer slab (tunable size, e.g., 32–256MB) and manages aliasing metadata. Exposes API: lease_acquire(tensor_id, mode), lease_release(tensor_id, status), stage_to_slab(tensor_id).
- Flow-control shim: central in-process coordinator per-node. Tracks per-device token buckets and queue depths. Exposes: request_preflight(request_meta) -> {placement, lease_strategy, estimated_penalty_ms}.
- Affinity probe: async sampler that inspects metrics from Triton/TensorRT endpoints (in-flight ops, kernel queue lengths, recent percentile latencies) and returns a quick score.
- Kernel adapter hooks: small changes in TRT/Triton adapters to honor leases and to accept shared-borrow views (zero-copy alias when allowed). For custom kernels, an adapter provides explicit copy-on-write semantics.

Operational flow (happy-path short decode)
1) Client request arrives and is routed to a worker. request_preflight runs (cheap), predicts placement on kernel A (e.g., TensorRT) with lease strategy = short-lease.
2) Kernel A acquires soft-owner lease for KV prefix tensors and operates in-place.
3) If decode completes quickly, lease_release happens; no transfers required.

Operational flow (cross-kernel handoff)
1) A downstream step requires a custom kernel (e.g., specialized attention transform). preflight decides custom kernel should run, but kernel queues show >80% utilization.
2) Flow-control shim instructs the custom kernel to either: take shared-borrow (if read-only), or use the staged transfer slot (if mutation required). stage_to_slab is invoked and the custom kernel consumes from slab asynchronously.
3) Lease-release includes a small lease token with a timeout — if the downstream kernel cannot complete before timeout, the shim triggers fallback routing to a compatible model variant.

KV cache implications
- KV lease model: per-request/sequence lease on KV shards. Short-lived leases for streaming sessions reduce cross-request contention.
- Prefix leasing: allow older KV prefixes to be demoted to read-only and shared-borrowable to support inference across kernel boundaries without copies.
- Stale eviction policy: combine access recency with predicted reuse from preflight probe so that rarely reused KV buckets get pushed to slower storage earlier, freeing slab space.

Tradeoffs observed in early experiments (summary)
- Latency: short requests (<=16 tokens) kept on primary kernel maintain 95th pct token latency similar to baseline (<5% regression). Handoff path introduces 2–8 ms extra latency depending on slab size and PCIe bandwidth.
- Throughput: modest improvement for mixed workloads because we avoid full kernel unloads, but worst-case throughput can regress if slab occupancy is undersized and causes repeated host-device transfers.
- Complexity: adapter changes for TensorRT/Triton are minimal (lease no-ops if unsupported) but custom kernels need explicit handling. Debugging lease races is the main complexity pain point.
- Memory overhead: the slab plus metadata adds steady-state overhead (tunable). For models with large KV state (>8GB), slab must be sized carefully or fall back to host transfer paths.

Key implementation details & heuristics
- Lease timeout default: 80ms for short-lease, 300ms for long-lease, application-configurable per-model.
- Slab sizing heuristic: 1% of device RAM or min(256MB, 0.02 * active_KV_size) — measured as reasonable starting point in our runs.
- Probe scoring: weighted sum of (kernel_queue_depth * 0.5) + (recent_p95_ms * 0.4) + (predicted_kv_hit_rate * -0.3). Tunable weights.
- Fallback policy: exponential backoff + rate-limited routing to quantized variant; after 3 consecutive timeouts consider dynamic model splice to cheaper variant.

Experiment notes (raw)
- Bench setup: A40 cluster, Triton serving two model variants (float16 TRT fused, and a custom CPU postprocess). We generated a mixed workload: 70% short-seq chat (avg 12 tokens), 25% long context (avg 1024 tokens), 5% embedding/rerank.
- Metrics: token-level tail latency, slab occupancy, PVC (PCIe) transfer bytes, kernel swap counts.
- Observations: small slab (64MB) caused transfer spikes and increased tail latency; 128MB provided stable tail but increased steady memory.
- Edge-case: synchronous small-runs where custom kernel expects writeable view caused OOM when allocator tried to alias; fixed by conservative promotion to staged copy for mutation cases.

Open questions / TODOs
- Should the slab be per-GPU or per-server with NUMA-aware pinning? Early tests show per-GPU is simpler and lower-latency but wastes memory for low-util servers.
- API surface: propose lease_* APIs be exposed in low-level runtime (C ABI) and wrapped by Triton/TRT adapters. Need to draft API proto.
- Correctness model: define strict invariants for aliasing vs copy-on-write to avoid subtle race conditions; formalize in a short spec.
- Observability: add lease lifecycle traces to Console and a per-request timeline that highlights cross-kernel transfers.

Recommended next steps
1) Small infra spike: implement sandwich allocator + slab on a single-worker dev image and wiring into the TRT adapter (no-op for Triton until adapter hooks in place). 2 engineer-weeks.
2) Add flow-control shim prototype (single-node, single-thread token bucket) and run mixed workload experiment. 2 engineer-weeks + 1 experiment week.
3) Expand to KV prefix lease tests with streaming sessions and measure tail latencies and slab pressure. 2 experiment weeks.

Appendix: quick sketch of lease API (informal)
- lease_acquire(request_id, tensor_id, mode: {read, write, shared}, timeout_ms) -> lease_token or error
- lease_release(lease_token, status: {done, handoff, error})
- stage_to_slab(tensor_id, lease_token) -> slab_handle
- slab_read(slab_handle) -> device_ptr (async)

Notes to reviewers
- This is intentionally a prototype-level doc: many heuristics are placeholders. Looking for feedback on the memory-sandwich idea, slab sizing heuristics, and whether we should prioritize per-GPU or per-node slab design.
- Related experiments: see linked GH PR for early allocator code and JIRA for scheduling tickets.

-- end --
